catalog_quote: Também o tom não é usado distintivamente na língua. Quando testado experimentalmente, o tom, no nível da palavra fonológica, mantém-se constantemente nivelado. [...] O acento é fixo. Há maior intensidade sempre na primeira sílaba da palavra fonológica, em conjunção com uma leve subida do pitch. A diferença entre uma sílaba acentuada e uma sílaba não-acentuada é mínima. Nos nossos registros, foram encontradas palavras de até cinco sílabas. Em todas, o acento recai sobre a primeira sílaba da esquerda. [...] Isso posto, parece não haver muito o que dizer sobre acento nessa língua. Tanto nomes como verbos mostraram o mesmo comportamento quanto ao padrão acentual. Podemos dizer, portanto, que Ofayé é uma língua de pés livres, ou seja, uma língua em que há apenas um acento por palavra e que coloca o núcleo acentuado na sílaba final ou inicial. new_statements.quote: O acento é fixo. Há maior intensidade sempre na primeira sílaba da palavra fonológica, em conjunção com uma leve subida do pitch. A diferença entre uma sílaba acentuada e uma sílaba não-acentuada é mínima. Nos nossos registros, foram encontradas palavras de até cinco sílabas. Em todas, o acento recai sobre a primeira sílaba da esquerda. [...] 1. a sílaba é a unidade portadora de acento; 2. o acento principal – talvez único – cai sobre a primeira sílaba à esquerda, ou seja, na sílaba inicial da palavra; 3. a segunda sílaba é mais fraca do que a primeira, mas mais forte do que todas as sílabas subsequentes; 4. palavras compostas seguem o mesmo padrão das palavras simples
new_statements.translation: Stress is fixed. There is always greater intensity on the first syllable of the phonological word, together with a slight rise in pitch. The difference between a stressed and an unstressed syllable is minimal. In our records words of up to five syllables were found; in all of them stress falls on the first syllable from the left. [...] 1. the syllable is the stress-bearing unit; 2. the main stress - perhaps the only one - falls on the leftmost syllable, i.e. the word-initial syllable; 3. the second syllable is weaker than the first but stronger than all subsequent syllables; 4. compound words follow the same pattern as simple words

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and fixed on the initial syllable of the phonological word (nouns and verbs alike, words of 1-5 syllables, compounds included); realized as slightly greater intensity plus a small pitch rise, with only a minimal stressed/unstressed difference. Tone and length are not distinctive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress posited ('o acento principal – talvez único'); only a gradient note that the second syllable is weaker than the first but stronger than all following syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: None lexical. Principle 5: in noun+adjective and possessor+possessed phrases each word keeps its own (initial) stress; footnote 29 (p. 89) says stress is the boundary signal of the phonological word, so an apparent multi-stress item like ['hie e'eti'to o] 'janela' is really three words. Author calls the description preliminary and notes rare pitch peaks are speaker emphasis.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (stress = its demarcative signal); data are elicited words and phrases from the last fluent speakers at Aldeia Anodi, Brasilândia (MS), early 2000s. CONFLICT to flag: Gudschinsky 1974 (pp. 180-182; one rememberer, 1968, isolated words) instead describes each root morpheme as heading its own stressed foot, words with several stresses and no single word apex, plus a high-to-low pitch contour (a morphologically determined / no-word-apex reading); Nikulin 2020 p. 97 regards Gudschinsky's 'stress' as simply the unmarked realization of full syllables. Oliveira's is the fuller, later, first-hand phonological analysis and is taken as the statement of record.
new_statements.identity_note: Both primary sources describe the single Ofayé variety (ofay1240, ISO opy) of the Ofayé(-Xavante) community at Brasilândia, Mato Grosso do Sul; no dialect split. Gudschinsky 1974 rests on one elderly rememberer recorded in 1968 (isolated words); Oliveira 2006 on the last handful of fluent speakers at Aldeia Anodi c. 2002-2005. 'Ofaié-Xavante' is unrelated to Xavante (xava1240, Central Jê).

sources.note: §1.6.1 'Tom e acento', pp. 89-92: duration and tone not phonological; stress is fixed, greater intensity always on the first syllable of the phonological word with slight pitch rise; difference between stressed and unstressed syllables minimal; words up to 5 syllables all stressed on leftmost syllable (examples 284-309); one stress per word; second syllable weaker than first but stronger than the rest; compounds follow same pattern; in N+Adj / possessive phrases each word keeps its own stress. Conclusion (p. ~247) repeats: tone has no role, Ofayé a 'língua de pés livres'.

sources.note: §1.4-1.5, pp. 180-182 (one elderly rememberer, 1968 fieldwork, mostly isolated words): a phonological word consists of one or more feet each marked by a stressed apex, so a word may have several stresses; no foot is uniformly or contrastively stronger than others (word has no single apex); most salient word feature is a high-to-low pitch pattern, highest pitch on first syllable or first stressed syllable; the foot nucleus (stressed) marks root morphemes (incl. augmentative/diminutive), unstressed affixes group rhythmically with the root. Note 7 p. 245: diminutive carries its own stress.

sources.note: §3.1.4 p. 97: sources on Ofayé are phonetically discrepant; he omits Gudschinsky's (1974) stress marks because in her data most polysyllabic words have multiple tonic syllables, 'sugerindo que a característica prosódica interpretada como acento tônico por Gudschinsky é a realização não marcada das sílabas na língua'; marks her unstressed vowels as reduced instead. No positive stress rule of his own.
